analysis.one_liner: Lets the Energy Secretary cap runaway wholesale electricity prices when federal regulators fail to act.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Energy Committee after a single March 2001 hearing; it never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: During the Western electricity crisis of 2000-01, when wholesale power prices in California and neighboring states spiked to many times their normal cost, this bill would have let the Secretary of Energy impose temporary regional caps on wholesale electricity prices. The caps would kick in when federal regulators found rates unjust or unreasonable, or when prices far exceeded the actual cost of producing power, and regulators had failed to act. Governors of states in the region could opt out.
analysis.who_benefits: Electricity consumers across the Western states, especially in California, who were paying the pass-through costs of soaring wholesale power prices, rationing, and utility bailouts during the crisis. The bill would have rolled wholesale rates back toward cost-of-service levels — the cost of producing power plus a fair return on invested capital [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The Secretary of Energy would be required to impose an interim regional price limitation — or a cost-of-service based rate — on wholesale electricity sales whenever rates are found unjust, unreasonable, or unduly preferential, or significantly exceed the marginal cost of production, and the high prices threaten public health, safety, or a regional economy while federal regulators have failed to act [S2] [S3].
The cost-of-service rate is defined to cover all fixed and variable production costs plus a return on invested capital — a regulated-utility standard, not a market spot price [S3].
The limitation would stay in effect until the Secretary determined the market reflected just and reasonable rates [S3].

It would apply across the Western Systems Coordinating Council region, with prices differentiated by season, time of day, and usage patterns, and governors of individual states could waive application within their states [S3].
Sales from small qualifying power and cogeneration facilities under the Public Utility Regulatory Policies Act would be exempt [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Wholesale electricity generators and power marketers, who would see their rates rolled back from crisis-inflated market prices to cost-based levels, reducing revenue on sales in the affected region.

drawbacks.text: Price caps set below market levels can discourage investment in new generation and, in a genuine supply shortage, can deepen the crunch rather than fix it — the central objection economists raised to wholesale caps during the Western crisis.

The bill concentrates sweeping authority in a single cabinet officer: the Secretary could override federal regulators, set rates for an entire multi-state region, and decide on his own when the market has returned to 'just and reasonable' rates [S3].
The governor opt-out could unravel the regional cap, since a single state's waiver would leave its utilities buying at uncapped prices while neighbors paid capped rates [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers in a region experiencing sustained price spikes and rolling blackouts, the protection promised was substantial and the caps were temporary and cost-based rather than punitive. The design weaknesses are real — heavy delegation to one official, a leaky opt-out, and the risk of chilling generation investment — but they are ordinary trade-offs of emergency price regulation, not flaws that sink the case for acting. The bill's practical problem was not its design but that it never advanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, sent to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, got one hearing in March 2001, and then sat without a committee vote or floor action until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill on January 22, 2001, at the height of the Western power crisis, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources [S1] [S5].
The committee held a single hearing on the bill on March 15, 2001, printed as S.Hrg. 107-49 [S5].
No markup, committee vote, or floor action followed; the bill's last recorded action was the March 2001 hearing, and it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wholesale electricity generators and power marketers came out ahead: no interim caps were enacted, so wholesale sales in the West continued at unregulated market rates. Electricity consumers did not receive the price protection this bill offered.

for.name: Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, held one hearing on March 15, 2001, and never voted to report it to the floor.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed imposing wholesale price caps in the Western electricity market during the 2000-01 crisis, arguing caps would not solve the supply problem, setting the administration's stance against the kind of intervention this bill required.

against.name: Wholesale electricity generators and power marketers
against.role: Sellers of wholesale power in the Western market
against.what_they_did: Fought against wholesale price caps during the Western crisis, arguing they would distort the newly deregulated market.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored by two California Democrats and drew no other cosponsors; it never reached a vote in either a Republican-led or Democratic-led Senate, so no party split was ever recorded.

industries.industry: Wholesale electricity generators and power marketers
industries.note: The bill would have rolled their wholesale rates back from crisis-inflated market prices to cost-based caps whenever prices threatened public health or a regional economy and regulators failed to act [S2] [S3]. Their revenue on Western sales depended on keeping prices uncapped, which put their interest directly against the consumers paying those prices.

The bill would have shifted rate-setting power from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to the Secretary of Energy when FERC had found rates unjust but failed to fix them [S2] [S3]. States gained a waiver right, but the executive branch gained authority at the regulator's expense.
